choices: Because the point is to stop giving equal status to every demand, not to become mechanically unavailable
Because blocked time should always be easy to discard
Because every request deserves equal access once the score is known

explanation.gentle: The chapter says intentionality protects what matters without turning boundaries into theater.
explanation.direct: The issue is selective access, not severe schedule performance for its own sake.
explanation.competitive: Good boundaries serve the work instead of trying to look impressive.

questions.prompt: What hard test sits underneath the chapter's protection warning?
choices: Whether yes/no discipline and blocked time actually change what the week allows
Whether the calendar contains enough blocks
Whether saying no feels comfortable enough socially

explanation.gentle: The chapter keeps asking whether protection becomes real in practice instead of staying verbal.
explanation.direct: The threshold is operational: do boundaries materially alter access to time and attention or not?
explanation.competitive: If the calendar still gets raided, the language was fake.

choices: A question of who owns the follow-through when the work is still difficult
A return to scorekeeping as the whole system
A decision to stop using boundaries because the week is now safe

coreSkill.gentle: The core skill is protecting important work through clearer yes/no choices and defended time.
coreSkill.direct: The core skill is turning priorities into protected priorities by controlling access to time and attention.
coreSkill.competitive: The edge is guarding the week before drift gets through the gate.

plan.gentle: If a work priority keeps getting crowded out, then identify what needs a no and what time needs protection before the week fills up.
plan.direct: If the calendar keeps yielding priority time to smaller requests, then use firmer yes/no decisions and defended blocks to change access.
plan.competitive: If the priority keeps getting raided, close the gates and guard the block.

plan.gentle: If study or project time keeps disappearing, then ask which extra commitments are taking space that the real work needed.
plan.direct: If school priorities stay clear but weak, then protect them with better no decisions and earlier claimed time.
plan.competitive: If the week keeps saying yes to everything else, make the real work a guarded territory.

plan.gentle: If a personal priority keeps waiting for leftovers, then block real time for it and defend that block when easier demands appear.
plan.direct: If intention stays verbal, then turn it into protected time and filtered access instead of hoping spare capacity appears.
plan.competitive: If the block keeps disappearing, treat it like territory and defend it.

twentyFourHourChallenge.gentle: Within the next 24 hours, choose one priority and decide what gets a no so that priority can keep its time.
twentyFourHourChallenge.direct: In the next day, protect one important block by deciding in advance which competing demands will not get access to it.
twentyFourHourChallenge.competitive: Before tomorrow ends, find one leak in the week and shut the gate.

weeklyPractice.gentle: Once this week, review whether your priorities were merely known or actually protected.
weeklyPractice.direct: Run a weekly access check: what got into the calendar, what should have been refused, and which blocks held under pressure?
weeklyPractice.competitive: Test the week. Did the guards hold, or did the same raiders get through again?

front.gentle: What problem does Chapter 7 solve after scorekeeping?
front.direct: Why is intentionality needed after visible truth?
front.competitive: What does the score still fail to defend?

back.gentle: It protects important work so the next week does not get crowded out again.
back.direct: Intentionality is needed because truth alone does not guard the next week from competing demands.
back.competitive: The score can expose the leak, but it cannot guard the calendar.

front.gentle: Why do yes and no matter here?
front.direct: How do yes/no choices affect execution?
front.competitive: What does every yes do to the week?

back.gentle: Because each yes gives something access to limited time and attention.
back.direct: Yes and no matter because capacity is limited and every admission affects execution quality.
back.competitive: Every yes opens the gate to something that costs the priority.

front.gentle: What is blocked time doing in this chapter?
front.direct: Why is blocking time more than decoration?
front.competitive: What turns the calendar into defended territory?

back.gentle: Blocked time gives important work protected space in the week.
back.direct: A block matters because it changes who gets access to time before the week gets negotiated away.
back.competitive: The block is supposed to guard the priority's ground.

front.direct: Why is the chapter not just arguing for rigid control?
front.competitive: What fake version of intentionality does the chapter reject?

back.gentle: Intentionality is selective protection, not rigid control for its own sake.
back.direct: The chapter wants disciplined boundaries that serve execution, not performative severity.
back.competitive: It rejects boundaries that look strong and still protect nothing.

front.gentle: What hard test does the chapter apply to intentionality?
front.direct: How do you know whether intentionality is real?
front.competitive: When does the chapter say the language is fake?

back.gentle: You know intentionality is real only when the week's access rules actually change.
back.direct: If yes/no choices and blocked time do not alter access to the week, then protection is still rhetorical.
back.competitive: If the week still gets raided, the language was fake.

keyTakeawayCard.gentle: Chapter 7 says seeing the truth is still not enough. Important work needs real protection through better yes/no choices and blocked time.
keyTakeawayCard.direct: The chapter's core move is turning known priorities into protected priorities. Intentionality matters because it changes what gets access to time and attention.
keyTakeawayCard.competitive: The score may expose the weakness, but boundaries are what stop the week from getting robbed again.
